  Terse gloss: "To sow seed; used of planting, of what is sown, and of the sower in parable"
  Readable gloss: "One of the New Testament's most vivid agricultural verbs, speiro describes the act of scattering seed onto prepared ground. Jesus made it central to his teaching through the Parable of the Sower (Matt 13:3-23), where the word itself appears in active, passive, and participial forms to describe the sower, the act of sowing, and the various fates of what is sown. Paul extends it powerfully in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 to describe the resurrection body 'sown in corruption, raised in incorruption,' and in Galatians 6:7-8 for sowing to flesh versus Spirit."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "sow seed, plant"
    Enriched: The active sense of scattering or planting seed, covering both literal agriculture (Matt 6:26, 'they neither sow nor reap') and figurative sowing of the gospel or of righteousness. The Spanish 'sembrar' and German 'saeen' faithfully mirror the base agricultural meaning. Jesus' parable begins with this act: 'a sower went out to sow' (Matt 13:3).
    Existing Spanish translations: sembramos, sembrar, sembraste, sembré, sembró, sembró-encima, siembra, siembran, siembras, siembre
  Sense 2: "be sown, what is sown"
    Enriched: The passive voice indicating what has been sown or planted, prominent in Jesus' interpretation of the parable where 'what was sown on rocky ground' represents a type of hearer (Matt 13:20). Paul's resurrection discourse in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 uses this form repeatedly: 'it is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption.' The Spanish passive 'es sembrado/a' precisely captures this grammatic...
    Existing Spanish translations: es-sembrada, es-sembrado, se-siembra, sembrada, sembrado, sembrados
  Sense 3: "the sower (substantival)"
    Enriched: The participial form used as a substantive noun meaning 'the sower,' a figure who becomes almost a title in Jesus' parables. In Matthew 13:3 the sower goes out, and in 13:37 Jesus identifies the sower as 'the Son of Man.' The consistent rendering across languages (Spanish 'que siembra,' English 'sower') shows how naturally the participle became a character designation.
    Existing Spanish translations: que-la-sembró, que-sembró, que-siembra, sembrador, sembrando
